title: Concept 17. Excessive Agency
summary: Excessive agency occurs when an AI agent has more permissions, capabilities or autonomy than it needs to complete its task.

sections.title: 1. What is excessive agency?
sections.body:
Excessive agency occurs when an AI agent has more permissions, capabilities or autonomy than it needs to complete its task.

In simple words:

**You give an AI agent too much power.**

Example:

You build a customer-support agent. It only needs to check order status, but you give it access to:

- Read all customer records.
- Delete customer accounts.
- Issue unlimited refunds.
- Modify payment details.
- Send emails to anyone.

That is excessive agency.

scenario.title: Scenario — Concept 17. Excessive Agency
scenario.situation: You build a customer-support agent. It only needs to check order status, but you give it access to: - Read all customer records. - Delete customer accounts. - Issue unlimited refunds. - Modify payment details. - Send emails to anyone. That is excessive agency.

choices.label: Ignore it and ship anyway
choices.explanation: Skipping detection leaves users exposed and makes root-cause analysis harder later.

choices.label: Add detection signals first
choices.explanation: Check these questions: - Does the agent have tools unrelated to its job? - Can it modify or delete data unnecessarily? - Can it perform irreversible actions? - Can it execute unlimited operations? - Can it access other agents' permissions? - Can it act without a human approval step? Perform capability and permission reviews for every agent.

choices.label: Apply a production fix / mitigation
choices.explanation: Apply layered mitigations, validate with tests, and monitor recovery.

sections.title: 3. Why does excessive agency happen?
sections.body:
Common causes:

1. Giving an agent access to every available tool.
2. Using administrator credentials for ordinary operations.
3. Allowing unlimited autonomous execution.
4. Failing to limit the number of tool calls.
5. Not requiring human approval for high-impact actions.
6. Allowing one agent to control another agent without restrictions.

sections.title: 4. Real-world scenario
sections.body:
Consider an AI employee-management agent.

User asks:

"Find employees who haven't completed compliance training."

Expected action: read employee training records and return a report.

But the agent also has access to `delete_employee()`.

A prompt injection or incorrect model decision could cause an unintended deletion.

The problem is not only the prompt. The agent has been given unnecessary authority.

sections.title: 5. How to detect excessive agency
sections.body:
Check these questions:

- Does the agent have tools unrelated to its job?
- Can it modify or delete data unnecessarily?
- Can it perform irreversible actions?
- Can it execute unlimited operations?
- Can it access other agents' permissions?
- Can it act without a human approval step?

Perform capability and permission reviews for every agent.

sections.title: 6. How to prevent it
sections.body:
Use these principles:

| Security control | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Least privilege | Give only required permissions |
| Tool allowlist | Restrict available functions |
| Scoped credentials | Limit access to specific resources |
| Action limits | Restrict quantity and frequency |
| Human approval | Review high-impact actions |
| Time limits | Prevent long-running autonomous behavior |
| Audit logs | Track all important actions |

sections.title: 7. Practical architecture
sections.body:
**AI Agent**

Decides what action is needed

↓

**Policy and permission engine**

Is this agent allowed to perform this action?

↓

**Low-risk action**

Execute within limits

**High-risk action**

Human approval

↓

**Controlled execution and audit**

**Interview question:** What is the difference between prompt injection and excessive agency?

**Answer:**

- Prompt injection is an attack that attempts to manipulate the model's behavior.
- Excessive agency is a design weakness in which the agent has more authority than necessary.

Prompt injection can exploit excessive agency, but they are different problems.

quiz.question: What is excessive agency?
options: It is the exposure of confidential or private information through prompts, retrieved context, model responses, logs or connected tools to unauthorized users or destinations.
Model extraction is an attack in which someone attempts to reproduce or approximate a proprietary model by repeatedly querying it and observing its outputs.
Data poisoning is an attack in which an attacker deliberately introduces malicious, misleading or manipulated data into the data used by an AI system.
Excessive agency occurs when an AI agent has more permissions, capabilities or autonomy than it needs to complete its task.
quiz.explanation: Excessive agency occurs when an AI agent has more permissions, capabilities or autonomy than it needs to complete its task. In simple words: You give an AI agent too much power. Example: You build a customer-support agent.

quiz.question: Why does excessive agency happen?
options: Because retrieved documents become part of the model's context.
Without proper tenant isolation: Company A might access Company B's documents; Company B might retrieve Company C's conversations; One tenant might delete another tenant's data.
Common causes include: Developers assume system prompts are private; Applications place sensitive information inside prompts; Prompt templates are accidentally returned in responses.
Common causes: Giving an agent access to every available tool; Using administrator credentials for ordinary operations; Allowing unlimited autonomous execution.
